inputs.need:
I am the clinical biochemist responsible for the diabetes tests at a regional laboratory that serves 64 primary care practices and two hospitals. About 18 percent of haemoglobin A1c requests from primary care arrive less than 80 days after the patient's previous result, and in most of those the earlier result was already stable. Repeating the test before the red cell population has turned over tells the clinician almost nothing new, costs reagent and phlebotomy time, and occasionally leads to a treatment change based on a difference within the analytical variation.

We would like to add a minimum retesting interval rule to the laboratory information system: a request for an HbA1c within 80 days of the previous result would be held rather than run, and the requesting clinician would get a comment explaining why, with a simple way to override for pregnancy, a new diagnosis, a recent transfusion or a treatment change. Before we switch it on for everyone, we want a feasibility study (a pilot at six practices for four months) to find out how often the rule fires, how often clinicians override it and why, whether the override route is quick enough, whether any held test delays a decision that matters, and whether practices find the comment acceptable.

I need help defining progression criteria for a wider rollout, deciding what to measure and how, choosing the six practices, and planning a safety review of held requests. The laboratory director has approved the rule in our test system; the primary care network's clinical governance committee has not yet agreed to it.
inputs.constraints: The pilot runs within existing laboratory and practice staff time. It must finish by 2027-05-31 so that a decision can be made before the next reagent contract. The rule can be switched on for named practices only, not for individual clinicians.
localFacts: The laboratory director approved configuration of the interval rule in the test system and for six named practices on 2026-09-03 (change request LAB-CR-2026-31).
The primary care network's clinical governance committee deferred its decision on 2026-09-10 and asked for a patient safety review of the override categories first.
Over the last 12 months the laboratory processed about 96,000 HbA1c requests from primary care; 18 percent arrived less than 80 days after the previous result.
The laboratory information system can hold a request, send a coded comment and record every override with the reason entered by the requester.

response.title: Feasibility of a minimum retesting interval rule for HbA1c in six primary care practices
response.subtitle: Four-month pilot with progression criteria before a network-wide rollout
response.statement: About 18 percent of primary care HbA1c requests arrive less than 80 days after the previous result, when a repeat adds little information and can prompt treatment changes within analytical variation. A laboratory rule that holds early requests, explains why and allows override is ready in the test system. It is not known how often the rule would fire in these practices, how often and why clinicians would override it, whether overrides would be fast enough, whether any hold would delay an important decision, or whether practices would accept it.

response.whatHurts: Early repeats cost patients extra blood draws and time, use reagent and staff time, and can lead to treatment changes based on noise. A badly designed hold could delay testing in pregnancy or after a treatment change.
response.currentPractice: All HbA1c requests are run whatever the interval; no comment explains retesting intervals.
response.whyNow: The rule is configured, the reagent contract decision is due in mid 2027, and the network committee wants safety evidence before agreeing.
response.patientCenteredGoal: People with diabetes have HbA1c measured when the result can change their care, and never have a needed test delayed.
response.summary: Problem framed as a feasibility question for an interval rule, with safety and acceptability as the decisive uncertainties.

records.title: A laboratory rule to hold early repeat HbA1c requests: before-and-after evaluation in primary care
records.authors: Mensah-Rydberg K, Oyelowo-Pratt D, Castaneda-Holm L
records.abstract: In one regional laboratory, a rule that held HbA1c requests made within 80 days of a previous result was introduced for all 48 primary care practices. Early repeat requests fell from 17 percent to 6 percent of HbA1c requests over 12 months. Clinicians overrode 4.3 percent of held requests, most often for pregnancy or a recent change in treatment. A review of 200 held requests found no case in which the hold delayed a treatment decision judged important by two diabetologists. Requesters complained mainly about the wording of the comment in the first two months after the rule started.

records.title: Minimum retesting intervals in clinical biochemistry: a consensus statement
records.abstract: A working group of laboratory professionals and clinicians agreed minimum retesting intervals for 24 common tests. For HbA1c, three months was agreed for monitoring established diabetes, with exceptions for pregnancy, suspected rapid change, new diagnosis and conditions affecting red cell turnover. The group advised that any hold rule must offer a simple override and that laboratories should review held requests for harm. Evidence for most intervals was indirect, and the statement relied on expert agreement for 19 of the 24 tests.

records.title: Why clinicians repeat HbA1c early: an analysis of override reasons under an interval rule
records.abstract: Across 18 practices using an interval rule, 1,905 held HbA1c requests were followed. Requesters overrode 212 (11.1 percent); the reason matched an accepted exception in 58 percent of overrides, and in the rest the most common reason was a patient appointment already booked. The median time from hold to override was 1 working day. Practices with a named diabetes nurse overrode less often. Overrides without an accepted reason clustered among a few clinicians, which suggests that feedback could be targeted.

records.title: Acceptability of laboratory demand management rules among primary care clinicians
records.authors: Ferreira-Lindgren M, Achebe-Nakamura J, Brandt-Oduya P
records.abstract: We surveyed 312 primary care clinicians and held group discussions with 26 in practices that had used laboratory hold rules for at least a year. Most accepted hold rules for tests they saw as low risk, but 39 percent felt that rules on diabetes monitoring interfered with their clinical judgement. Acceptance was higher when the comment explained the reason in one sentence and gave the override route. Clinicians wanted the rule to recognise pregnancy and recent treatment changes automatically where the record allowed it.

records.title: Concentration of early repeat HbA1c testing among primary care practices: implications for targeting
records.abstract: Using two years of laboratory data from 70 practices, we found that the 10 percent of practices with the most early repeat HbA1c requests accounted for 38 percent of all early repeats. Early repeats were more common where results were requested by practice-based pharmacists and in practices with high locum use. Practices whose recall systems booked diabetes reviews at fixed three-month intervals also had more early repeats. Targeting feedback to high-repeat practices reduced early repeats by a third in a small follow-up. The analysis could not examine individual clinical reasons for repeat requests.

response.synthesis: Five retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A hold rule cut early repeat HbA1c requests from 17 to 6 percent in one laboratory without important delays in 200 reviewed holds, and override analyses elsewhere give planning values (about 11 percent overridden, median 1 working day). A consensus statement defines exceptions and asks for harm review. Acceptability is uncertain: 39 percent of clinicians felt diabetes monitoring rules interfered with judgement. Early repeats concentrate in a minority of practices. The evidence supports a small pilot with explicit progression criteria and a safety review, not immediate rollout.
response.gradeRationale: Uncontrolled evaluations, a consensus statement and a survey; consistent but indirect for these practices, and too small to exclude rare harm.
response.summary: Five records appraised; five claims; overall certainty low.

response.reading: An early repeat request is the product of practice routines (booked reviews, pharmacist requesting, locum cover) meeting a laboratory that runs every request. The hold rule moves the decision to the moment of request and adds an override, so its feasibility depends on how quickly clinicians can override for real exceptions and on whether they accept the comment. Safety depends on the exception categories. Practice variation means the pilot must include both high-repeat and typical practices.

response.overview: Four-month feasibility pilot (January to April 2027) of a laboratory hold rule for HbA1c requests within 80 days of the previous result in six primary care practices, with progression criteria for network rollout and a safety review of held requests.
response.population: All HbA1c requests from six practices: three from the highest decile of early repeat requesting and three typical practices, of mixed size and rurality; requests from hospitals are excluded.
response.exposure: Hold rule: a request within 80 days is held and a one-sentence comment explains the retesting interval and gives the override route (reply code with a reason: pregnancy, new diagnosis, recent transfusion or blood loss, treatment change in the last 8 weeks, other).
response.procedures: The rule is switched on for the six practices only after network committee agreement. Every hold and override is logged by the laboratory information system. A diabetologist and a practice pharmacist review every held request followed by a treatment change within 30 days, every override without an accepted reason, and a random 10 percent of other holds. Requesters complete a five-question acceptability survey in month four. Progression criteria are fixed before the rule starts.

response.designSummary: Single-arm feasibility pilot judged against pre-specified progression criteria; no hypothesis tests.
response.sampleSize: Six practices produce about 3,000 HbA1c requests in four months (about 96,000 a year across 64 practices). With 18 percent early requests, about 540 holds are expected; with about 11 percent overridden (c3), about 60 overrides. If 90 percent are completed within one working day, 60 overrides give a 95 percent confidence interval of about 82 to 98 percent, enough to tell whether the threshold is plausibly met. Zero important delays among about 540 holds would put the upper 95 percent bound for the delay rate near 0.6 percent (rule of three).
response.primaryAnalysis: Proportion of overrides for accepted exceptions completed within one working day with a Wilson 95 percent confidence interval, compared descriptively with the 90 percent threshold.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Firing and override rates by practice and month; override reasons; safety review counts with the rule-of-three bound; acceptability proportion; second draws.
response.missingData: Overrides without a recorded time are reported as not timely in a sensitivity count; unreturned surveys are reported by practice and role.
response.multiplicity: Progression criteria are judged together as pre-specified; no significance testing.
response.software: Laboratory information system extracts summarised in R.
overfittingGuards: No post hoc change of the 80-day interval during the pilot
response.summary: About 60 overrides and 540 holds; interval estimates against fixed thresholds.

response.risks: Low: a held test could delay a needed result; mitigated by the override route, exception categories and monthly safety review.
response.consent: The rule changes a laboratory process for practices, not individual care decisions; practices opt in through their lead clinician and patients are informed through practice notices. Requesters take part in the survey voluntarily.
response.data: Hold and override logs contain request identifiers; the review team sees only what is needed to judge delay; reports are aggregated by practice.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: people in rural practices, people who need interpreters and people with limited time off work bear the cost of any extra blood draw. Second draws are counted and reported by practice rurality, and the exception list includes conditions such as haemoglobinopathies and pregnancy that affect some ethnic groups more.
response.effectiveness: The pilot informs a rollout decision; failing a progression criterion leads to revising the rule or dropping the hold in favour of a comment.
response.efficiency: Saves reagent and phlebotomy time if it proceeds; the pilot uses existing staff.
response.costs: Reviewer and analyst time within existing roles; no new software.
response.partnerships: Primary care network clinical governance committee, two practice pharmacists, a diabetologist and two patient partners from the diabetes patient group.
response.rebPath: Screened as service evaluation by the laboratory's governance office; the network committee's agreement is required before the rule starts, following ICH-GCP and Declaration of Helsinki principles for confidentiality.
response.limitations: Six practices and four months; rare harms undetectable; practices know they are observed.
response.summary: Low-risk service pilot conditional on network agreement, with a safety review and attention to extra blood draws.

response.partnershipPlan: Two patient partners and two practice pharmacists review the comment wording and the override route before the pilot.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; the laboratory's user feedback inbox for the last year is read for comments on repeat testing.

response.title: Feasibility of a laboratory hold rule for early repeat HbA1c requests in primary care: a four-month pilot
response.abstract: Objective: to test the feasibility and safety of holding HbA1c requests made within 80 days of the previous result. Design: single-arm pilot in six practices with pre-specified progression criteria. Measures: timely overrides, safety review of held requests, firing and override rates, acceptability and second blood draws. Results will be written after the pilot.
response.introduction: Early repeat HbA1c testing adds little information and can prompt treatment changes within analytical variation. Hold rules reduce it elsewhere, but their safety and acceptance in primary care are uncertain.
response.methods: The rule held requests within 80 days and offered a coded override. Every hold and override was logged; two reviewers judged delays; requesters were surveyed at four months.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present each progression criterion with its interval estimate.
response.discussion: The discussion will state whether each progression criterion was met and what changes to the rule, the comment or the override route are needed. It will compare override behaviour with the retrieved reports.
response.limitations: Six practices over four months cannot detect rare harms, and there is no control group. Practices knew they were observed.
response.conclusion: To be written after the pilot. It will recommend rollout, revision or a comment-only approach against the pre-specified criteria.
response.reportingChecklist: CONSORT extension for pilot and feasibility studies (non-randomised adaptation)
